items.title: Trying to Cure My Cystic Fibrosis
items.why: A first-person essay by a patient-researcher on why CFTR modulators leave some people with CF behind, and why delivery (viral vectors vs. lipid nanoparticles, mucus, basal cells) is the hard part of gene therapy. It is one author's perspective, and the company clinical data it mentions are described as ambiguous and company-reported.
items.takeaway: Modulators need a broken CFTR protein to act on, so the 5–10% of patients with nonsense or frameshift mutations (no protein made) need other approaches such as gene therapy or editing.

items.title: Naked antisense oligonucleotides access the cytosol during early endocytic trafficking
items.by: Sitarska, E.; Saminathan, A.; Scanavachi, G.; Somerville, E.; Stock, P.; Shen, P.; Kahne, D.; Courtney, M. F.; Reid, D. A.; Danielsen, M. B.; Davidsen, F. K. N.
items.why: Live-cell imaging study of where naked antisense oligonucleotides actually reach the cytosol, relevant to how oligo therapeutics are interpreted. It is a bioRxiv preprint, not peer reviewed, with results mainly from cultured cells (U2OS).
items.takeaway: The authors report under 4% of internalized ASO reaching the nucleus despite >90% Malat1 knockdown, and place productive escape early in endocytic trafficking.

items.title: A low-rank decoder bottleneck bounds reliability in foundation-model perturbation prediction
items.by: Zheyu Zhang, Yuanhao Huang, Fan Feng, Jie Liu
items.why: Asks when a single-cell perturbation-prediction model's output can be trusted for choosing experiments, rather than relying only on aggregate accuracy. Preprint; the numbers below come from the abstract and are the authors' own audit of the STATE decoder.
items.takeaway: The abstract reports that a predicted-NN-distance confidence score tracks per-perturbation Pearson delta correlation (mean absolute Spearman 0.81).

items.title: Atom14 and Atom37: how protein design models write down atoms
items.why: A clear explanation of how protein design models represent atoms when the sequence is not yet known, comparing RFdiffusion3, BoltzGen and La-Proteina. It is useful for reading protein generative-model papers; the RFdiffusion3 and BoltzGen papers it cites are bioRxiv preprints.
items.takeaway: Atom14 and Atom37 are residue-aware layouts, so each design model needs its own way to carry unknown residue identity through generation.

items.title: Stop using win rate: comparing model rankings across different benchmark tasks
items.why: A short, practical argument against reporting win rate alone in model benchmarks, with runnable code on simulated data. The example is simulated, and the post is aimed at cheminformatics benchmarks, but the statistics carry over to any multi-task evaluation.
items.takeaway: In the simulated example, a model with an 80% win rate could not be statistically separated from the others once tests across tasks were applied.

items.title: The AlphaFold2 Method Paper: A Fount of Good Ideas
items.why: An expert reading of the AlphaFold2 architecture that focuses on transferable design ideas, such as the 1D/2D representation split and information flow. It pairs well with the Atom14/Atom37 post, since AF2 is where that layout is used. The author notes his interpretation may be wrong.
items.takeaway: The author argues the single-sequence representation, not an explicit 3D computation, carries the structure, with the pair representation acting as memory.

items.title: Diffusion is spectral autoregression
items.why: A signal-processing explanation of why image diffusion behaves like coarse-to-fine autoregression, with a reproducible notebook. It builds durable intuition about generative modelling that carries over to scientific data.
items.takeaway: Natural image spectra follow an approximate power law while Gaussian noise is flat, so added noise acts roughly like a low-pass filter whose cutoff depends on the noise level.

items.title: Feature Visualization
items.by: Chris Olah, Alexander Mordvintsev, Ludwig Schubert
items.why: A rigorous Distill treatment of interpreting neural networks by optimizing inputs, covering objectives, diversity and why individual neurons may not be the right unit. It is background for interpretability work on any model, including biological ones.
items.takeaway: Optimization separates what causes a neuron to fire from what merely correlates with it, but a single optimized example can mislead without diversity.

items.title: Visualizing Representations: Deep Learning and Human Beings
items.why: Colah's classic on using dimensionality reduction to inspect learned representations, with a caution that axes in t-SNE plots carry little meaning. It is a useful grounding for reading embedding plots, including single-cell ones.
items.takeaway: In a t-SNE plot the meaningful information is mainly which points sit close together, not the axes.

earlier.title: The Future of Protein Science will not be Supervised
earlier.why: Makes the case for global, semi-supervised representations of protein sequence space (UniRep). Argues that the gap between available sequences and labelled data makes proteins a good domain for them. It is a 2019 opinion post on a preprint, so treat its predictions as the author's views.
earlier.takeaway: The author reports that a single UniRep neuron could partly distinguish alpha helices from beta strands (ρ = 0.33).

earlier.title: Visual Information Theory
earlier.why: Evergreen visual explanation of probability, codes and entropy, building towards information theory. A foundational read that is still useful for loss functions and representation learning.
earlier.takeaway: Entropy is the fundamental limit on average message length; in the example, 1.75 bits is the best possible for that distribution.
